newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Ruehe to visit Africa for security talks.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Ruehe to visit Africa for security talks.

text.p: Germany's Defence Minister Volker Ruehe leaves on Sunday for a five-day tour of southern Africa where he plans to discuss regional security and improve top-level contacts.

Ruehe arrives in Namibia, a former German colony, on Monday before travelling on to neighbouring South Africa and then to Zimbawe. It will be the first official visit of a German defence minister to the region, a ministry spokesman said.

"Ruehe will meet top heads of state for talks, but they are not planning to sign any cooperation agreements," the spokesman said, adding that the tour reflected Germany's growing interest in global security issues.
Arms or military cooperation, he said, were not on the agenda.
Ruehe will meet Namibian President Sam Nujoma, Prime Minister Hage Geingob and Defence Minister Phillemon Malima for talks in Windhoek.
Later on Monday he flies to Cape Town, South Africa, where he will meet President Nelson Mandela, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, Defence Minister Joe Modise and Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo.
The visit to South Africa is the latest in a series of top-level contacts between the two countries since the end of apartheid.

Mandela, on a visit to Germany last May aimed at boosting trade, hailed Chancellor Helmut Kohl's commitment to strengthening bilateral co-operation in the post-apartheid era. Kohl became the first German leader to visit South Africa in 1992.

Apart from security issues, diplomats said Ruehe was likely to talk about the problems his own country has faced integrating the armed forces of former Soviet satellite East Germany into the German federal army.

The issue is close to South Africans' hearts because of their efforts to integrate guerrilla fighters from the African National Congress (ANC) -- now the ruling party -- and the Pan African Congress into the country's armed forces, once their sworn enemy.
"They will probably exchange information and experience on this," said the spokesman. "But no one is making a direct comparison between military integration in Germany and South Africa."

Ruehe is due to fly to the town of Phalaborwa near the Mozambique border some 300 km (200 miles) northeast of Johannesburg to inspect Special Forces Regiment 5 based there -- one of new South Africa's top military units.
The unit is composed mainly of black commandos who undergo a rigorous 49-week selection course which turns down some 90 percent of applicants.

The unit developed from one set up in 1976 in which black troops were trained to infiltrate liberation groups like the ANC and the South West African People's Organisation (SWAPO) which was fighting Pretoria's control of what is now Namibia.
